pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Types of Rock — the three main kinds: igneous (lava/magma cools and hardens), sedimentary (layers of material pressed together), and metamorphic (heat and pressure change existing rock); fossils are found in sedimentary rock.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement — note the mismatch):** DfE Y3 **Rocks** (statutory) is: "compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties"; "describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock"; "recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter." Crucially, the NAMES igneous/sedimentary/metamorphic and the rock cycle are NOT KS2 statutory — 'sedimentary rock' appears only in the non-statutory notes (fossils context), and the three rock types + rock cycle are formally DfE **KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere**. So this topic teaches KS3 vocabulary using a KS2-appropriate hands-on approach; treat naming as enrichment atop the statutory 'compare/group + fossils' work.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No elementary PE names the three rock types; rock/soil formation and change connect to **4-ESS1-1** and **4-ESS2** (evidence of change; weathering/erosion). Rock formation processes are developed at **MS-ESS2**. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Earth Is Made of Rock' and 'What Is a Volcano' (igneous links to cooled lava). Two facets: (1) classify real rocks by appearance/properties (statutory KS2 skill — grains vs crystals, layers, fossils), and (2) the big idea that rock TYPE encodes how it FORMED. Land the load-bearing link: fossils are found in sedimentary rock BECAUSE it forms gently in layers — things can be trapped and preserved — whereas igneous rock forms from melt that would destroy them.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A/B (classify by observable properties; begin process→product reasoning). Children can sort by look/feel and match a type to its formation with support, but tend to treat 'rock' as one undifferentiated material and to think all rocks contain fossils. Success = name the three types, state igneous forms from cooled lava/magma, and explain fossils are in sedimentary rock because it forms in layers.
bestPractices: Ground naming in hands-on classification first (hand lens: grains vs crystals, visible layers, fossils) — the statutory KS2 skill — then attach the type name to what was observed.
Teach each type by its FORMATION STORY, not just a label: igneous = melt cooled and hardened; sedimentary = layers of bits pressed together; metamorphic = existing rock changed by heat and pressure.
Make the fossils–sedimentary link causal, not a coincidence: gentle layering can trap and preserve remains; melting (igneous) and intense heat/pressure (metamorphic) would destroy them.
Use real specimens (granite, sandstone/chalk, marble/slate) and building stones/gravestones so classification is evidential and local (links to Geography).
Address the 'rock = human-made too' misconception (Oak National Academy): brick, tarmac and concrete are manufactured, not natural rock — sort natural vs made.
keyRepresentations: A 'rock factory' with three formation processes: cooling melt → igneous; pressing layers → sedimentary (with a trapped shell); heat+squeeze → metamorphic
Real rock specimens examined with a hand lens (crystals vs grains vs layers vs fossils)
Sedimentary layers building up with a shell caught between them → revealed as a fossil
commonMisconceptions: All rock is basically the same material (there are distinct types formed by distinct processes).
All rocks contain fossils / fossils can be in any rock (fossils are found in sedimentary rock because it forms in gentle layers).
Brick, concrete and tarmac are kinds of rock (they are human-made materials, not natural rock).
Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic are just names to memorise (each name IS its formation story).
Rocks never change from one type to another (they can, very slowly — the rock cycle, taught next at 9–11).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: learn the three main rock types — igneous (melt cools and hardens), sedimentary (layers of material pressed together), metamorphic (existing rock changed by heat and pressure) — and that fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock BECAUSE it forms gently in layers that can trap and preserve remains, whereas melting destroys remains and intense heat/pressure usually destroys or badly squashes them. Ground the naming in hands-on classification of real specimens first (grains vs crystals vs layers vs bands vs fossils), then attach each name as shorthand for its formation story. Note the standards context: classifying rocks and describing fossil formation is the statutory KS2 skill, while the three type-names and rock cycle are formally KS3 vocabulary taught here as enrichment atop that hands-on work.

activities.title: Run the rock factory: make each type and test what survives
feedback: If the shell burns away in the lava and is crushed/smeared in the heat-press but survives in the layers, that is exactly why fossils are found in sedimentary rock — not by coincidence but because of how each rock forms.
If you expected a fossil in the igneous rock: igneous forms from hot melt that would destroy a once-living thing; only the gentle layering step keeps a shell intact.
Tie the name back to what you did: 'sedimentary' = layers that settled and were pressed; 'igneous' = melt that cooled; 'metamorphic' = rock changed by heat and pressure.
activities.rationale: Doing each formation process and testing shell survival turns 'fossils are found in sedimentary rock' from a fact to memorise into a conclusion the learner reaches, and makes the causal link (gentle layering preserves; heat destroys) concrete.
sourceClaims: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma/lava; sedimentary from compacted layers of sediment (fossil-bearing); metamorphic from heat and pressure altering existing rock.
learnerActions: At a 'melt' step, cool a glowing lava/magma pool and watch crystals lock together, forming igneous rock.

At a 'layers' step, drop layers of sand and mud with a small shell tucked between them, press them down to make sedimentary rock, then split it open to reveal the shell as a fossil. (In real rock, hardening the layers and turning a shell into a fossil takes a very long time.)

At a 'heat and squeeze' step, take an existing rock and increase heat and pressure until it changes, for example its minerals lining up in bands, forming metamorphic rock (many, though not all, metamorphic rocks show bands).
Try to preserve a shell in each process: drop it into the lava, put it through the heat-and-press, and set it among gentle layers — observe which process preserves it and which destroy it.
State in your own words why fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock: why melting in igneous rock destroys them, and why heat and pressure in metamorphic rock usually destroy or squash them.
activities.intendedInsight: A rock's type is its formation story, and fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock because gentle layering can trap and preserve remains, while melting (igneous) destroys them and intense heat/pressure (metamorphic) usually destroys or distorts them.

activities.title: Hand-lens classification of real specimens
feedback: If you grouped a specimen by a single feature, check a second property with the lens — grains (which may rub off) or visible layers/fossils point toward sedimentary, interlocking crystals of mixed colours toward igneous, and bands or thin splitting sheets toward many metamorphic rocks. Remember marble is metamorphic yet crystalline and usually has no bands, so tell it apart from igneous rock by its mostly single-coloured crystals, its softness, and its fizzing in vinegar.
Name the type only after describing what you saw, so the label stays tied to the evidence.
Using real building stones or gravestones shows these rock types are all around you, not just in a classroom.
activities.rationale: Hands-on classification by observable properties is the statutory KS2 skill and gives an evidential foundation before type-names are attached.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 'Rocks' statutory objectives: compare/group rocks by appearance and simple physical properties; describe how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock; recognise soils are made from rocks and organic matter. The named three rock types + rock cycle are KS3 Chemistry, not KS2.
learnerActions: Examine real rock specimens such as granite, sandstone or chalk, and marble or slate with a hand lens.
Look for distinguishing clues: interlocking crystals, loose grains, visible layers, embedded fossils, or bands/stripes (foliation).

Sort the specimens into igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic based on what you observe, then say which clue led to each decision. (Note crystals can appear in both igneous rock such as granite and some metamorphic rock such as marble. Marble usually has no bands, so compare the crystals instead: granite has mixed colours, marble is mostly one pale colour. With an adult, you can also check whether it fizzes in vinegar.)
Where possible, link to local examples such as building stones or gravestones.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks can be compared and grouped by their appearance and simple physical properties, and the observable texture (crystals, grains, layers, bands, fossils) is evidence of how the rock formed.

activities.title: Natural rock or made by people?
feedback: If you called brick a rock: brick, concrete and tarmac are made by people, while rocks form through natural processes like cooling, layering, or heat and pressure.
A good test is to ask: did this form in nature, or did someone manufacture it?
activities.rationale: Directly targets the common belief that manufactured materials are kinds of rock, keeping the natural/made distinction explicit.
sourceClaims: A common Y3 misconception is that manufactured materials (brick, tarmac, concrete) are rock; teaching should distinguish natural rock from human-made materials.
learnerActions: Look at a mixed set including natural rocks (granite, sandstone) and manufactured materials (brick, tarmac, concrete).
Sort each item into 'natural rock' or 'made by people'.
Give a reason for each sort, focusing on whether the material formed by a natural process or was manufactured.
activities.intendedInsight: Brick, concrete and tarmac are human-made materials, not natural rock, even though they can look rock-like.

activities.title: Explore examples and consolidate naming
feedback: For the fossil question, a full answer names sedimentary AND gives the reason (gentle layers trap and preserve remains).
If a match is wrong, revisit the formation story: melt → igneous, pressed layers → sedimentary, heat and pressure → metamorphic.
These grouping and matching tasks check what you already understand; they work best after doing the formation processes rather than instead of them.
activities.rationale: Reading formation facts and grouping/matching consolidates naming and classification, but checks rather than generates the causal insight, so it follows the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma/lava; sedimentary from compacted layers of sediment (fossil-bearing); metamorphic from heat and pressure altering existing rock.
learnerActions: Explore examples of the three rock types; for each, find out how it formed and where it is found.

Look closely at the distinguishing texture of each: crystals (igneous), layers with a fossil (sedimentary), bands or thin splitting sheets in many metamorphic rocks such as gneiss or slate (though marble has crystals and usually no bands).
Answer the question: 'Which rock holds fossils, and why?'
Consolidate by grouping specimen images by type, matching each type to its formation process, and answering: 'In which rock would you find a fossil, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: The three names are shorthand for distinct formation processes, and fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock because of its gentle layered formation.

constraints: Grouping, matching and short-answer consolidation checks and assesses understanding but does not, on its own, elicit the learner's independent construction of the causal fossils-in-sedimentary reasoning; use it after the hands-on formation work.

A view-only presentation conveys the naming and classification half well but presents the causal fossils link as a stated fact; learners benefit from also running or observing the formation contrast to reach it themselves.

Rotating/zooming 3D specimens can aid close observation of texture, but rock-type learning does not hinge on 3D spatial reasoning; a 2D view with hand-lens zoom is sufficient, so treat 3D as an optional enhancement.

Keep the formation mechanisms distinct: igneous = cooled melt, sedimentary = pressed layers, metamorphic = existing rock changed by heat and pressure (often, but not always, showing bands; marble usually has none). Do not let the layering idea bleed into igneous.

Crystalline texture is not unique to igneous rock (some metamorphic rock such as marble is crystalline). Banding helps identify some metamorphic rocks (e.g. gneiss), but marble usually has no bands, so separate it from igneous rock such as granite using other clues: marble's crystals are mostly one pale colour, it is softer (a steel nail can scratch it), and it fizzes in vinegar (adult-led), whereas granite has crystals of mixed colours and does not fizz.

The three type-names and the rock cycle are enrichment (formally KS3) layered on top of the statutory KS2 skills of classifying rocks and describing fossil formation; prerequisites include understanding that Earth is made of rock and what a volcano is (igneous links to cooled lava).

The rock cycle (one type changing into another over long timescales) is formally taught later, at KS3 (ages 11–14); here, note only that rocks can change very slowly, without developing the full cycle.

Simulated melting/pressure stations model what would happen to a fossil; use them as representations of real geological processes, not as literal claims that every fossil in every real setting is always destroyed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (Oak National Academy misconception guidance; USGS/BGS rock-type claim) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE standards claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The source states intense heat/pressure (metamorphic) and melting (igneous) destroy fossils; real geology is more nuanced (some fossils can partially survive mild metamorphism). The 'usually destroys' framing in the assessment answer is a reasonable simplification for ages 7–9; keep it as a strong general rule rather than an absolute law.
The standards note flags a KS2/KS3 placement mismatch (three type-names are formally KS3); preserved as context so teaching treats naming as enrichment atop statutory work.

Crystalline texture overlaps igneous and some metamorphic rock (e.g. marble); the hand-lens clues add banding to keep the metamorphic category identifiable, an age-appropriate simplification not independently source-verified.
Product/UI mechanic vocabulary (gallery, lift-the-flap, tap/zoom/drill-down) and quiz-step labels were reworded into descriptive learner actions in the final guidance.

probeDeeper: How does sedimentary rock form, step by step — and why does that let a fossil survive?
What would happen to a fish's body if it were caught in hot lava that then cooled into igneous rock?
Is a brick a rock? Why or why not?
Name the three rock types and give one way each is different.
assess.correctAnswer: Sedimentary rock. It forms gently, as layers of sediment settle and press together over time, so a buried animal or plant can be preserved as a fossil inside the layers. Igneous rock forms from hot melted rock (lava/magma cooling), which would destroy a fossil; metamorphic rock is changed by great heat and pressure, which also usually destroys fossils.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fossils can be found equally in any type of rock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link formation to survival — heat and melting destroy fossils; only gentle layered sedimentary rock preserves them.
errorPatterns.distractor: It doesn't matter — fossils are found in all three types equally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks igneous/metamorphic, or says it doesn't matter which type.

errorPatterns.pattern: Igneous rock forms from squashed layers / all rocks form by layers pressing (muddles formation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Igneous = cooled lava/magma; sedimentary = pressed layers — keep the mechanisms distinct.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's igneous — because igneous rock forms from layers pressing together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says igneous forms from pressed layers rather than cooled melt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Manufactured materials like brick, concrete or tarmac are types of rock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rocks are natural; brick, concrete and tarmac are made by people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies man-made materials as natural rock.

responseLevels.gap: Can't name the types, or thinks fossils occur in any rock; may call brick a rock.
responseLevels.full: Identifies sedimentary and explains its gentle layered formation preserves fossils whereas igneous (cooled melt) and metamorphic (heat/pressure) destroy them — and distinguishes natural rock from manufactured materials.
responseLevels.partial: Names the three types and says fossils are in sedimentary but can't explain why (the gentle-layering vs heat contrast).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A fossil of a fish is found inside a rock. Which of the three rock types — igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic — is it most likely to be in, and WHY does that type keep fossils safe while the others usually don't?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can recite the three names yet not connect how each type FORMS to whether a fossil survives. Asking why sedimentary keeps fossils forces the gentle-layering mechanism contrasted with heat destroying them — separating memorised names from understanding formation.
